nodes.trigger: when a problem requires reordering characters into groups while preserving the original relative order within each group
nodes.content: Use stable partition via two separate sequential filter-then-concatenate passes rather than in-place swaps or unstable partitioning. Collect group A characters in input order into one list, collect group B characters in input order into another list, then concatenate A+B. Because both passes traverse the original sequence in order, relative order within each group is automatically preserved without needing a stable-sort comparator.
nodes.purpose: Guarantee order-preservation without complex comparisons or extra sort overhead
steps: Identify the partition predicate (e.g., is-digit vs not)
Traverse input once appending matching elements to list A
Traverse input once appending non-matching elements to list B
Return concatenation of A followed by B
nodes.negative_example: Do not use Python's sorted/sort with key returning 0/1 unless the sort is guaranteed stable and the predicate is well-defined; do not use in-place swap partitioning which loses relative order

nodes.trigger: when a competitive-programming problem refers to 'digit characters' and input is ASCII but the language has Unicode-aware built-ins
nodes.content: Prefer an explicit ASCII digit-set membership test over str.isdigit() when the problem intends only '0'-'9'. str.isdigit() returns True for Unicode superscripts, subscript digits, and other non-ASCII digit code points, which can cause wrong answers on edge test cases containing such characters. An explicit ASCII set is unambiguous and matches judge expectations.
nodes.purpose: Avoid false-positive digit detection from Unicode-only digit code points
steps: Confirm the problem means ASCII 0-9
Check membership against an explicit set of the ten ASCII digits or use a range check like '0'<=c<='9'
Avoid isdigit/isnumeric for the partition predicate unless Unicode digits are explicitly required
nodes.negative_example: Do not blindly use str.isdigit() as the digit predicate in algorithmic problems sourced from online judges expecting ASCII semantics
constraints: input may contain non-ASCII or special Unicode characters that isdigit misclassifies

nodes.trigger: when reading single-line string input that may carry trailing newlines or carriage returns from different platforms
nodes.content: Normalize line endings before partitioning by removing carriage returns entirely and stripping trailing newline characters from the raw input. This prevents stray control characters from being treated as part of the data string on Windows-based judges or judges that append CRLF. Apply normalization to the input string at the start of the solve function so both the test harness entry and the stdin entry behave identically.
nodes.purpose: Prevent trailing CR/LF from being misclassified as non-digit characters and corrupting output
steps: Replace all carriage-return characters with empty string
Right-strip newline characters
Use the cleaned string as the working data for all subsequent logic
nodes.negative_example: Do not strip with a broad whitespace rstrip() if internal spaces are meaningful; do not assume input has no trailing newline because judges often append one
constraints: input is a single logical line
internal content must be preserved exactly

nodes.trigger: when a submission must satisfy both a local pytest harness importing a solve function and an online judge reading stdin
nodes.content: Provide dual entry points in the solution module: a pure solve(input_text) function that returns the result string, plus a guarded __main__ block that reads from stdin and prints the result. The function signature is what the test harness imports; the __main__ block is what the online judge executes. This lets the same file pass local tests and judge execution without modification.
nodes.purpose: Make one solution file work for both local parametrized testing and online judge stdin/stdout
steps: Define solve(input_text) returning the output string with no side effects
Add a guard block that reads sys.stdin.read(), calls solve, and prints the result
Ensure print adds exactly one trailing newline as judges typically expect
nodes.negative_example: Do not put input-reading logic inside solve itself; do not omit the __main__ guard or the harness import will trigger stdin reads during collection

nodes.trigger: when a task-completion signal is emitted before verification actually confirms success, leading to repeated or premature completion markers
nodes.content: Emit the task-completion signal exactly once, and only after the verification command (e.g., pytest with non-zero exit check) has returned success. If the signal must be re-emitted due to external coordination, first re-run the verification command to confirm state is still valid. Premature completion markers waste cycles and risk false-success reporting if the environment changed.
nodes.purpose: Ensure completion signals reflect verified passing state rather than optimistic assumptions
steps: Run the verification command capturing its exit code
Only if exit code is zero, emit the completion signal once
If forced to re-emit, re-run verification immediately before each re-emission
nodes.negative_example: Do not echo a completion marker multiple times in sequence without re-verifying between them; do not emit completion before the test run has finished
constraints: completion signal should be emitted at most once per genuinely verified state

nodes.trigger: when validating a stable-partition or character-reordering solution with a small manual test set
nodes.content: Augment the minimal provided test cases with boundary-category inputs that exercise the partition predicate and order preservation: empty string, all-digit string, all-nondigit string, a single-character input, and an input containing consecutive same-class characters clustered together. These reveal off-by-one, empty-list concatenation, and order-preservation bugs that the happy-path example will miss.
nodes.purpose: Catch partition edge cases that the single provided example cannot expose
steps: Add an empty-string case asserting empty output
Add an all-digit case asserting output equals input
Add an all-nondigit case asserting output equals input
Add a case with multi-character digit clusters verifying intra-cluster order is preserved
Add a case with a trailing newline to confirm input normalization
nodes.negative_example: Do not rely solely on the problem's single worked example to validate correctness; do not add cases that duplicate coverage already provided by existing cases
constraints: each added case should cover a distinct category not already exercised

nodes.trigger: When a shortest-path problem restricts certain nodes from being intermediate stops but exempts the source and/or destination from the restriction
nodes.content: Run standard Dijkstra but apply the forbidden-node filter only during edge relaxation: skip relaxing into a neighbor if it is forbidden AND not the destination. Enqueue the source unconditionally regardless of its forbidden status. This precisely enforces 'forbidden nodes may appear only as endpoints'.
nodes.purpose: Correctly implement path constraints that apply only to intermediate nodes without special-casing the graph structure
steps: Enqueue source into the priority queue without any forbidden-set check
During neighbor relaxation, skip neighbor v if v is forbidden and v != destination
Allow relaxation into destination even if destination is in the forbidden set
nodes.negative_example: Do not pre-remove forbidden nodes from the adjacency list or skip the source if it is forbidden — this would incorrectly block valid paths where the source or destination itself is forbidden

nodes.trigger: When running Dijkstra and only the single-pair shortest path is needed (source to one target)
nodes.content: Break out of the main loop immediately when the target node is popped from the priority queue. Dijkstra guarantees the first time a node is popped its distance is final, so this yields the correct answer without processing remaining heap entries.
nodes.purpose: Reduce runtime by avoiding unnecessary relaxation of nodes extracted after the target
steps: After popping (dist, node) from heap and passing the stale-check, test if node == target
If so, break the loop and return the recorded distance
nodes.negative_example: Do not break when the target's distance is first updated during relaxation — only break when it is popped, because a later shorter path may still exist in the heap

nodes.trigger: When performing frequent membership tests inside the inner relaxation loop of a graph algorithm and node IDs are dense integers from 1 to n
nodes.content: Use a boolean lookup array indexed by node ID instead of a hash set for forbidden/visited/active node membership tests. Array indexing has no hash overhead and better cache locality.
nodes.purpose: Eliminate per-edge hash-set overhead in hot inner loops
steps: Allocate a boolean array of size n+1 initialized to False
Mark forbidden nodes to True during input parsing
Test membership via direct array indexing in the relaxation loop
nodes.negative_example: Using a Python set for membership tests when n is up to 1e5 and the test runs inside an O(m) loop adds avoidable constant-factor overhead

nodes.trigger: When the source and destination may be the same node in a shortest-path problem
nodes.content: Check for source == destination before any graph initialization or traversal and return zero immediately. This avoids issues where the source might be filtered out or where no edges exist.
nodes.purpose: Correctly handle the degenerate same-node case and skip unnecessary computation
steps: After parsing source and destination, compare them
If equal, return the trivial zero-distance result before building adjacency lists
nodes.negative_example: Null — this is a safe guard clause with no downside
constraints: source and destination share the same node space

nodes.trigger: When parsing competitive-programming input with irregular line breaks or mixed whitespace
nodes.content: Tokenize the entire input string via split() and consume tokens with an index pointer rather than reading line by line. This is robust to arbitrary whitespace and line-break variations between test judges.
nodes.purpose: Avoid input-parsing failures due to line-break format differences
steps: Read the full input text, call split() to get a flat token list
Use a mutable index counter to Sequentially consume integers
Advance the index by exactly the number of tokens consumed for each field
nodes.negative_example: Do not assume one logical value per line or use fixed readline counts — judges may format input differently from the sample

nodes.trigger: When using a priority queue with potential stale entries due to multiple pushes of the same node
nodes.content: After popping an entry from the heap, compare its stored distance against the current best-known distance array. If the popped distance is greater, skip processing (lazy deletion). This avoids the need for a decrease-key operation.
nodes.purpose: Maintain correctness and efficiency when using a binary heap without decrease-key support
steps: After popping (d, u), check if d > dist[u]
If so, continue to the next iteration without relaxing u's edges
Only relax edges for entries whose distance matches the current best
nodes.negative_example: Do not process every popped entry without the stale check — stale entries waste time and can cause incorrect behavior if dist is used after popping

nodes.trigger: Solving a 'move certain characters to one end while preserving relative order within each group' problem
nodes.content: Use stable partition via two-pass filtering: first pass collects all characters that stay, second pass collects all characters that move; concatenate the two lists. List comprehensions over the original string preserve intra-group relative order automatically.
nodes.purpose: Produce a correct stable-partition result in linear time with clean, readable code
steps: Identify the predicate separating the two character groups
Build group A (the ones that stay) by filtering on NOT predicate
Build group B (the ones that move) by filtering on predicate
Return concatenation A + B
nodes.negative_example: Do not sort or reorder within either group; do not use a single pass with index manipulation that risks breaking stability
constraints: preserve original relative order within each group

nodes.trigger: Problem says 'digit characters' (数字字符) and code uses Python str.isdigit() to classify digits
nodes.content: str.isdigit() returns True for non-ASCII Unicode digits such as superscripts (²), full-width digits, and Roman numeral characters. For competitive programming problems where 'digit' means ASCII 0-9 only, replace isdigit() with an explicit ASCII digit check to avoid hidden test failures.
nodes.purpose: Prevent misclassification of Unicode digit-like characters as digits in online judge hidden tests
steps: Detect that str.isdigit() is being used for digit classification
Replace with c in '0123456789' or equivalent explicit ASCII range check
Re-run tests to confirm behavior unchanged on existing cases
nodes.negative_example: Do not assume str.isdigit() only matches 0-9 in Python; it has broad Unicode coverage by design
constraints: OJ problems typically mean ASCII digits unless stated otherwise

nodes.trigger: Reading line-based input and stripping trailing newlines before processing
nodes.content:
Prefer rstrip('
') over strip('
') when the problem guarantees one line of input and leading characters are significant. strip('
') removes newlines from both ends, which can silently discard a leading newline if it were part of the data. Use strip('
') only when the entire input is a single line read that may have surrounding whitespace artifacts.
nodes.purpose: Avoid unintended removal of significant leading characters in line-based input handling
steps: Check whether problem states input is exactly one line with significant content
If only trailing newline from input() or readlines() is expected, use rstrip('\n')
If input may contain surrounding artifacts from file reads, strip('\n') is acceptable
nodes.negative_example: Do not use strip('\n') blindly when the problem does not guarantee the first character is not a newline

nodes.trigger: Designing test cases for a string transformation problem with character classification
nodes.content: Beyond the provided example cases, include tests for: empty string, all-one-category (all digits / all non-digits), single character, characters that are whitespace or special symbols, and alternating pattern. These cover the partition boundaries and confirm stability of intra-group ordering.
nodes.purpose: Achieve regression protection against hidden edge cases in online judge evaluation
steps: List all character categories the problem distinguishes
Add a case with each category alone (all digits, all non-digits)
Add a case with empty string and single character
Add a case with whitespace and special symbols mixed in
Add a case with alternating pattern to verify stability
nodes.negative_example: Do not test only the problem's example and one trivial variation; partition logic can fail silently on empty or single-category inputs

nodes.trigger: Problem requires moving one character class to the end of a string while preserving all relative orders
nodes.content: Two-pass stable partition is the simplest correct approach: O(n) time, O(n) space, and trivially correct. For n < 100 constraints, no in-place or single-pass optimization is warranted. Prefer code clarity over micro-optimization.
nodes.purpose: Select the simplest correct algorithm that handles the constraint scale without overengineering
steps: Verify the constraint size (small n means no need for in-place or streaming)
Implement two-pass filtering with concatenation
Confirm both groups preserve original order by construction
nodes.negative_example: Do not implement in-place pointer swaps or single-pass dual-collection unless the problem demands O(1) space or streaming

nodes.trigger: Solution passes all provided/local tests but reviewer flags potential Unicode character classification mismatch for online judge hidden tests
nodes.content: When local tests pass but reviewer identifies a semantic mismatch between the problem's implied character set (ASCII) and the Python built-in used (str.isdigit, str.isalpha, etc.), treat this as a latent failure risk. Replace the broad Python built-in with an explicit character-set check before submitting to the judge.
nodes.purpose: Eliminate latent failures from Python built-in character classification matching more than the problem intends
steps: Identify which Python built-in (isdigit, isalpha, isalnum, etc.) is used for character classification
Determine the exact character set the problem implies (typically ASCII)
Replace with explicit set membership or range check
Re-run tests and submit
nodes.negative_example: Do not assume passing provided examples means the classification is correct; Python built-ins have Unicode semantics that examples may not exercise
